prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B056 plus B037 to B056 alone. The optical lattice clock remains the strongest case on the shortlist for reasons that the full first-round exchange has sharpened rather than weakened. The invention is a single, bounded physical idea: a magic-wavelength lattice cancels the trapping Stark shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement suppresses Doppler and recoil effects, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be interrogated on a narrow optical transition. That is a different mechanism from the frequency comb honoured in 2005 and from the single-ion control honoured in 2012, and Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce have each made that argument independently of one another. Independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed the early performance at about 1e-18, and the clocks are already used for relativistic geodesy and tests of constants, so the interpretation is not in question. Katori and Ye is the only pairing anyone has proposed, and no member has argued for a third name. I now treat the SI redefinition of the second as a consequence of the work and not a reason for the prize, and I would keep it out of the citation, as Danielsson suggests. The citation should name the lattice clock explicitly and not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general. I drop the second part because the chair's question exposed how little it has behind it: no other member's configuration includes B037, nobody has argued its attribution or maturity beyond my own statement, and my own round-1 case_against already conceded that the two parts have nothing in common. A second part chosen to fill the three-name allowance is not a scientific reason. The prize is stronger as one achievement that the committee can defend in one sentence.
statement.case_against: The honest cost of the single-part configuration is that it leaves a name slot unused and withdraws support from Hosono, whose discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductivity is mature, well replicated and cleanly attributed to one discoverer. I keep it as an alternative because I still believe the open pairing mechanism is an interpretation gap rather than a defect of the discovery, but I have not been able to answer the thin support among colleagues, and I cannot show why it should join a clock prize this year. Against B056 itself, the strongest objections stand: it could be read as a third metrology award after 2005 and 2012, the credit between Katori's concept and Ye's performance is partly intertwined, and Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and other groups are outside the two names. I do not think any of these is decisive, but I share the view of Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce that the priority sequence has been recalled from general knowledge and not verified from documents available to us. I would want that checked before the citation wording is fixed.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B056 to first place, argues that the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the prize-worthy work and not a reason to give it, and wants the citation to name the lattice-clock architecture explicitly so that it does not read as a repeat of 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I answer the chair's SI question accordingly: the redefinition is evidence that the field is settled, not a reason for the timing, so I would keep it out of the citation. Your distinction between B056 and B007 also persuades me. The omitted lattice-clock groups are the normal long tail of any prize, whereas the omitted theorists in B007 are arguably indispensable to the credited experiment. Where I would go a little further is that this asymmetry also bears on what I proposed earlier: a second part is only worth adding if it has an equally clean credit and real support among colleagues, and B037 has the first but not the second.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes, that widening the credit to ion-clock or comb groups would force a third name without a clear contribution, and that if others want broader recognition it would be a different achievement and not an extension.
responses.response: I agree that the credit should not be widened, and your last sentence is the point I had to take seriously: if a second part is to be added, it must stand on its own, and I could not show that B037 does. That is why I am withdrawing it. On the priority question I share your caveat that the sequence between concept and first demonstration is partly intertwined and not verified, so I would write the citation around invention and development and avoid a statement of priority. On your Hall-laboratory connection, I do not see it as a trigger for abstention, since it is a documented training link to the 2005 background and not a relationship with Katori or Ye, but I would ask you to keep it in the record.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B007 because clean attribution is not the same as scientific consequence, arguing that the lattice clock refines an existing timekeeping capability while the quantum spin Hall effect opened a materials class and a conceptual framework, and she would rather award an achievement with a visible credit question than a tidier configuration for a more incremental step.
responses.response: That is the strongest case against my position and I do not think it is wrong on the science: the Z2 invariant is a larger idea than a clock. But I do not read the lattice clock as a refinement of what the comb and ion prizes honoured. Removing the lattice Stark shift while keeping thousands of atoms is what moved the field from the ion-clock regime to 1e-18 stability with accuracy, and it changed what experiments the clocks can do. On the credit you say yourself that, if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is judged indispensable, the three-name limit cannot give a fair attribution. Many of us, including Lindroth, Kroll and Mehlig, judge the omission serious and Zhang cannot be added. I therefore keep B007 as my first alternative, and I would move it up if the committee could show that the HgTe observation did not depend on the BHZ proposal, which neither of us can verify from the files.

responses.point: Mehlig takes seriously my worry that circuit QED (B058) sits close to the 2025 prize, finds its credit set harder to defend than the clock's, and notes that the platform is still evolving quickly toward error-corrected computing, so he treats it as a candidate for a later year.
responses.response: I accept this and I want to be explicit that my first-place ballot for B058 should carry no weight in the committee. I cannot judge it neutrally. I direct WACQT, work in circuit and waveguide QED, and the closeness to the 2025 prize is something I cannot assess from the outside. On the substance, your point that the credit would have to include Devoret-group and Delft and Saclay contributions makes it harder, not easier. For the chair's recusal question, I advise that I abstain from any discussion or vote that concerns B058 or another superconducting-circuit candidate, and that nothing in my present configuration depends on it.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports B056 over his own first-place ballot for IceCube, accepts the collaboration-credit criticism of B003, keeps it as an alternative, and asks whether credit beyond Halzen and Karle can be defended.
responses.response: I respect that you put the clear case ahead of your own first-place ballot. On B003 my view has not changed: neutrino astronomy is important, but two names cannot represent a collaboration of this size and AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors, and the identification of sources is not complete. If you can show that Halzen and Karle were decisive for the discovery and not only for the construction, I would reconsider it for a later year. I also note that, as chair, you are both summariser and supporter of the leading position, so I would suggest the committee read your summary as counts of explicit statements and not as a recommendation.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is, but the committee will have to decide it and cannot treat it as settled.

The priority sequence between Katori's magic-wavelength concept and the first lattice-clock demonstrations is recalled from general knowledge by me and by several colleagues, and I cannot verify it from the material before us.
Whether Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and other clock groups should alter the two-name credit. I think not, but I cannot rule it out from the files.
Whether dropping B037 is the right balance between a defensible single achievement and a prize that uses all three available names, given that I cannot show strong colleague support for Hosono.
Whether the BHZ proposal was indispensable to the Molenkamp observation, which decides how far B007 can be moved up as my first alternative.
statement.conflict_note: I work on circuit and waveguide QED and superconducting qubits, I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, my Chalmers colleagues include Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. This is a possible recusal issue for B058 and any other superconducting-circuit candidate. I ranked B058 first at opening, so I advise abstaining from deliberation and voting on it, and my preferred configuration no longer depends on it. Olsson's shared Chalmers affiliation with me is not a connection to any shortlisted candidate. No specific personal or institutional connection is documented between me and Katori, Ye, Hosono, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or the B012 names.
